blogDrafts.title: Start with one small coding win
blogDrafts.author: Nuevo Foundation workshop example
blogDrafts.summary: Give a new learner one visible change to make, then invite them to explain what happened.
paragraphs: A blank page can feel intimidating. Start with a tiny, visible outcome: change a heading, move a shape, or make a button respond. Ask the learner to predict what will happen before they run the code.

When the result appears, pause. Invite the learner to describe which line caused the change. Then ask for one variation of their own. The goal of this sample exercise is not speed or a perfect page. It is a small connection between an idea, a change, and something the learner can observe.
Keep the next step optional and specific. For example, ask them to choose a new label for the button, rather than redesigning the entire site at once.

blogDrafts.title: Debug with observations, not guesses
blogDrafts.author: Nuevo Foundation workshop example
blogDrafts.summary: Turn a confusing result into a repeatable observation and a smaller experiment.
paragraphs: When a page behaves unexpectedly, first describe what you expected and what you actually saw. Include the action that caused it and whether you can reproduce it.

Change one thing at a time. If a button does not respond, check that the button exists, that its label is clear, and that the event handler points to the intended element. A smaller experiment makes it easier to connect cause and effect.
After the fix, repeat the original action. Also try a nearby case, such as activating the button with a keyboard. Write down the observation instead of simply saying that everything works.

blogDrafts.title: Ship a change with a useful record
blogDrafts.author: Nuevo Foundation workshop example
blogDrafts.summary: Connect a feature request to its implementation, checks, and real delivery evidence.
paragraphs: A useful delivery record helps the next volunteer understand why a change exists. Start with a short problem statement and acceptance criteria that someone can check.
Keep the implementation focused. Review the files you intend to commit, run the relevant checks, and link the result to its issue. A local commit and a deployed feature are different states.

Finish by recording what changed, why it mattered, which checks actually ran, and where the published change can be found. If something remains blocked, leave that visible rather than treating a draft as a completed delivery.

concepts.name: Instructions
concepts.meaning: Standing guidance about how work should be done in a repository.
concepts.nfExample: Use approved NF facts and track feature work before implementing it.
concepts.boundary: Model guidance is not a security or enforcement guarantee.

concepts.name: Prompts
concepts.meaning: The task and context you give the agent for this interaction.
concepts.nfExample: Add the three impact values from this local PM brief.
concepts.boundary: A reusable prompt file is a client-specific convenience, not automatically a CLI command.

concepts.name: Agents
concepts.meaning: A focused role with instructions and a configured set of tools.
concepts.nfExample: An issue triager proposes labels for at most five issues.
concepts.boundary: A role name does not guarantee expertise, isolation, or permission.

concepts.name: SKILLS
concepts.meaning: A discoverable package of instructions and optional resources for a repeatable procedure.
concepts.nfExample: The issue-lifecycle SKILL carries a feature from an issue through verification and an evidence-backed finish.
concepts.boundary: Natural-language selection can vary. Explicit invocation and inspection are useful fallbacks.

concepts.name: Hooks
concepts.meaning: Code that runs at a supported tool or session lifecycle event.
concepts.nfExample: A bounded pre-tool check rejects a simple git commit command whose literal message lacks an issue reference.
concepts.boundary: Coverage is limited by the hook, parser, event, timeout behavior, and client. It is not universal enforcement.

concepts.name: MCP
concepts.meaning: Model Context Protocol exposes external tools and resources through a standard interface.
concepts.nfExample: Approved GitHub tools can read or update an issue when the account and tool permissions allow it.
concepts.boundary: A connection supplies capabilities, not permission or a workflow. GitHub CLI is an alternative for this lab.

concepts.name: LSP
concepts.meaning: Language Server Protocol supplies language-aware services such as diagnostics, symbols, and definitions.
concepts.nfExample: A configured language server helps navigate and diagnose a larger website's code.
concepts.boundary: The language server and client integration must exist. LSP does not replace testing or model judgment.

concepts.name: Plugins
concepts.meaning: A compatible bundle that can carry several customization components together.
concepts.nfExample: Package the delivery SKILL with a task command, triage agent, and bounded hook.
concepts.boundary: A plugin packages components; it does not grant their permissions or make every client's schemas identical.

concepts.name: Marketplace
concepts.meaning: A catalog used to discover and distribute compatible plugins.
concepts.nfExample: An approved team catalog can point to a reviewed version of the NF workflow plugin.
concepts.boundary: Catalog availability does not prove trust. Review the source and organization policy before installing.

lesson.title: Nine tools for a repeatable coding workflow
lesson.requestVsRecipe: A prompt is the order: cook dinner. A SKILL is the reusable recipe and procedure. Instructions are the kitchen's standing rules. An agent is a focused role, such as the prep cook. The analogy explains roles, not implementation boundaries.
lesson.practicePrompt: Preview how you would add grounded impact counters with the issue-lifecycle SKILL. Do not edit files or change GitHub.

quiz.question: Which concept carries the reusable issue-to-evidence procedure?

lesson.prerequisites: Reading the lesson needs only a browser. A real hosted GitHub Copilot CLI exercise also needs an approved account and permitted model-service connectivity.

faq.question: What does Nuevo Foundation help learners explore?
faq.answer: Its programs introduce learners to STEM through coding activities and conversations with people in the field.

faq.question: Which kinds of programs appear on the NF website?
faq.answer: The source website describes coding workshops, virtual sessions, and a speaker series.

faq.question: Which coding topics are mentioned?
faq.answer: Scratch, Python, JavaScript, HTML/CSS, and C# are listed in the source description of coding workshops.

faq.question: How can volunteers contribute?
faq.answer: The source website lists creating curriculum, helping with a workshop, and hosting a virtual session as volunteer paths.

faq.question: Can this practice site register me for a real program?
faq.answer: No. This is a local workshop canvas. It does not submit registrations, send messages, or collect personal information.

faq.question: Are the impact figures live?
faq.answer: No. They are a dated snapshot from the public website source. This exercise does not connect to an operational reporting system.
